newsitem.title: UK: EMU may prompt Europe gold reserve sales - analyst.
newsitem.headline: EMU may prompt Europe gold reserve sales - analyst.

text.p: European nations keen to join the first wave of the European Monetary Union (EMU) may be tempted to sell gold reserves early next year to meet EMU rules on their debt levels, a report from investment bank SBC Warburg said.
Such sales are likely to depress the price of gold, says Stephen Yorke, Warburg director of political research, author of the report which was published on Wednesday.

"As the Buba and others toughen their rhetoric on what member states have to do to quality for EMU this note raises the spectre of EU member state Central Banks selling gold reserves for a one-off fiscal windfall," he wrote.
"As we near the early-1998 EMU assessment period the temptation for some countries to raid their gold reserves to reduce debt in 1997 may be overwhelming."

France, holding the EU's largest percentage of gold in its foreign reserves, was the most likely to be tempted to sell gold, Yorke's report said. Italy, the Netherlands, Germany and Portugal were next in line.
Recent market talk of possible central bank sales has helped depress the price of gold, which crumbled below the $380 an ounce support level on Wednesday afternoon.
A precedent for such sales was set by Belgium, which sold 5.2 million ounces of gold reserves this year to help reduce debt for EMU qualification, Yorke said.
But although the Belgian sales had little effect on the gold market, the sale of gold reserves by other European banks might not be so benign, he added.

"The point is it's such an illiquid market that if the central banks start stealthily selling gold in the first and second quarters of next year, there won't be time to match supply and demand," Yorke said.
